why_how.text: Your condition and your attention both shape how safely you drive, and the manual names specific distractions to avoid.
Phone rules depend on your age, and screens and loud sound systems are illegal.

scenario.text: A seventeen-year-old driver gets a call and has a hands-free accessory in the car.

reasoning.text: Drivers under eighteen years of age may not use a cell phone or any other mobile electronic device while driving; the hands-free option is only for drivers eighteen or older.

result.text: The driver leaves the phone off or in the back seat and does not take the call while driving.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a hands-free accessory makes phone use legal for every driver.

correction.text: A driver under eighteen may not use a phone at all while driving, while a driver eighteen or older may use one only through a hands-free accessory.

memory_support.text: Under eighteen, phone away; adults, hands-free only.

prompt.text: How loud may a car stereo be before it breaks the law?

answer.text: Not loud enough to be heard fifty feet from your vehicle.

rationale.text: It is illegal to play a sound system loud enough to be heard fifty feet from your vehicle, since you need to hear horns, screeching tires and sirens.

lines.text: Health and emotions shape your driving.

narration.text: Your mental and emotional state and your physical health shape how you drive. Poor health, fatigue, or feelings such as anger or worry can make you unsafe. The manual gives a clear test for one warning sign: if you notice you are just going through the motions without really tracking what is happening around you, stop to rest or end your driving for the day. This lesson then turns to the distractions the manual names, including the phone rules that depend on your age, screens and loud sound systems, and things you hold or reach for while driving.

lines.text: Under eighteen: no phone or device.

narration.text: Phone rules in Oregon depend on your age. Drivers under eighteen years of age may not use a cell phone or any other mobile electronic device while driving, so turn it off or put it in the back seat. Drivers eighteen or older may use a cell phone or other mobile electronic device only with a hands-free accessory that needs no more than minimal finger use to switch on or off. So the under-eighteen rule is a complete ban while driving, and the adult rule allows only hands-free use with minimal finger use, never holding the phone.

lines.text: No video display the driver can see.
No sound heard fifty feet away.

narration.text: Two more rules are written into law. It is illegal to have a TV, tablet or other video display where the driver can see it. And it is illegal to play a radio or other sound system loud enough to be heard fifty feet from your vehicle, since you need to hear horns, screeching tires and sirens. So a screen showing video belongs out of the driver's view, and the volume stays low enough that the sounds of the road reach you. Both are illegal, and the sound rule exists so that you can hear horns, screeching tires and sirens. Keep that rule in mind.

lines.text: Nothing in your lap or arms.

narration.text: Anything that takes your eyes off the road while driving is dangerous, such as texting, reading, eating, drinking, putting on makeup or taking off clothing. Never hold a person, a pet or a package in your lap or arms while driving. And do not turn around to tend to passengers, children or pets. If they need attention, pull to the side of the road and park first. Each of these rules keeps your eyes on the road and your hands free to drive, and when something needs your attention, the answer is to stop the vehicle before you deal with it.

lines.text: Hands-free is not for under eighteen.
Under eighteen means no phone use.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A young driver believes that a hands-free accessory makes any phone call legal. That is true only for drivers eighteen or older. A driver under eighteen may not use a phone at all while driving, while a driver eighteen or older may use one only through a hands-free accessory that needs no more than minimal finger use. So the same phone, the same car and the same accessory can be legal for one driver and illegal for another, depending only on age. If you are under eighteen, the phone stays off or in the back seat.

Here is a quick check: you enjoy loud music in the car. At what point does the volume break the law? The answer is when the sound system can be heard fifty feet from your vehicle. It is illegal to play a radio or other sound system that loud, since you need to hear horns, screeching tires and sirens. Pair that with the screen rule: a TV, tablet or other video display must not be where the driver can see it. Both rules exist in the manual so that the sights and sounds of the road reach you. Keep that rule in mind. That is the rule to remember.

lines.text: Rest if you are on autopilot.
Phones by age, no screens, quiet enough.

narration.text: To wrap up: your health and emotions shape your driving, and if you find yourself going through the motions, stop to rest or end your driving for the day. Under eighteen, no phone or mobile device while driving; eighteen or older, hands-free only. No video display where the driver can see it, and no sound system loud enough to be heard fifty feet away. Avoid anything that takes your eyes off the road, never hold a person, pet or package while driving, and pull over and park before tending to passengers, children or pets.

why_how.text: Aggressive drivers and drowsiness are two of the biggest risks the manual describes, and each has a clear response.
Your health and your hearing affect your driving too.

scenario.text: You start yawning and drifting toward the lane line, and you are close to your destination.

reasoning.text: Yawning and drifting out of your lane are signs you may be falling asleep, and you should never keep driving drowsy just to reach your destination.

result.text: You pull over somewhere safe to rest, or get out for a brisk walk.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking it is fine to push on while drowsy if the destination is close.

correction.text: Never keep driving drowsy just to reach your destination; pull over somewhere safe to rest, or get out for a brisk walk.

memory_support.text: Yawns and drifting mean pull over.

prompt.text: An aggressive driver tailgates you and flashes lights. How should you respond?

answer.text: Stay out of the way and do not challenge the driver.

rationale.text: If you meet an aggressive driver, stay out of the way and do not challenge them by speeding up or trying to out-drive them.

narration.text: This lesson covers three conditions that can make driving unsafe: anger from other drivers, your own fatigue, and your health. Road rage is angry or aggressive behavior by drivers, such as driving in an illegal, unsafe or threatening way, shouting or making rude gestures. Fatigue has clear warning signs and clear responses. Health matters too, from being sick to medical conditions that affect driving, and so does your hearing. For each one, the manual tells you what to look for and what to do, and we will go through those steps in order.

lines.text: Do not speed up or out-drive them.

narration.text: If you meet an aggressive driver, stay out of the way and do not challenge them by speeding up or trying to out-drive them. Remember what road rage looks like: driving in an illegal, unsafe or threatening way, shouting, or making rude gestures. When you see those behaviors, the manual's response is to give that driver room and not engage. Speeding up or trying to out-drive the other driver is exactly the challenge the manual tells you not to make. Your goal is to let the aggressive driver go and keep your own driving calm.

Frequent yawning, head nodding, heavy eyelids, blurred vision and drifting out of your lane are signs you may be falling asleep at the wheel. A tired driver reacts more slowly and notices changing road and traffic conditions less. So be well rested before and during a trip, and take breaks when you feel tired. Be wary of medicines that can make you drowsy. When you notice those signs, the manual asks you to act: pull over somewhere safe to rest, or get out for a brisk walk, rather than keep going. Keep that rule in mind.

lines.text: Pull over to rest or walk.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A driver feels drowsy but is close to home and decides to push on. The manual says never keep driving drowsy just to reach your destination. Pull over somewhere safe to rest, or get out for a brisk walk. To stay awake on a trip, drink water, because dehydration causes fatigue, talk with your passenger, and take turns driving so each driver can rest. None of these replaces rest when the warning signs appear. A short distance left is not a reason to keep going while you are yawning, nodding or drifting. Keep that rule in mind.

lines.text: Judge whether you are fit when sick.

narration.text: If you are sick, think honestly about whether you are fit to drive, especially for a long trip. Some medical conditions can cause confusion, slower reaction time or a sudden loss of consciousness, so ask your doctor how your condition may affect your driving. Hearing matters while driving: tire noise changes with the road surface, engine noise can signal a problem, sound can reveal a vehicle in your blind spot, and you need to hear emergency vehicles. So do not wear headphones that could reduce your hearing while driving.

Here is a quick check: a driver behind you is tailgating, flashing lights and making rude gestures. How should you respond? The answer is to stay out of the way and not challenge the driver. The manual says that if you meet an aggressive driver, you stay out of the way and do not challenge them by speeding up or trying to out-drive them. Shouting, rude gestures and threatening driving are all part of road rage, and none of them call for a response in kind. Let the driver go and keep your own driving calm. Keep that rule in mind.

lines.text: Rest at the first signs of drowsiness.

narration.text: To finish: when you meet an aggressive driver, stay out of the way and do not challenge them. Watch for the signs of falling asleep, such as yawning, nodding, heavy eyelids, blurred vision and drifting, and never keep driving drowsy just to reach your destination. Be well rested, take breaks, drink water, talk with a passenger, take turns driving and be wary of drowsy medicines. When sick, judge honestly whether you are fit to drive, ask your doctor about medical conditions, and do not wear headphones that could reduce your hearing.

why_how.text: Alcohol and other drugs raise your chance of a collision that can cause serious injury or death.
DUII is about being affected, and it covers any substance, including medicines.

scenario.text: A driver has a blood alcohol concentration below zero point zero eight percent, but alcohol is clearly affecting their driving.

reasoning.text: At zero point zero eight percent or more the law presumes impairment, yet a driver below that level can still be arrested for DUII if alcohol or drugs are affecting their driving.

result.text: The driver can still be arrested for DUII even though the level is below zero point zero eight percent.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you cannot be arrested for DUII below zero point zero eight percent.

correction.text: You can still be arrested with a blood alcohol concentration below zero point zero eight percent if alcohol or drugs are affecting your driving.

memory_support.text: Affected means arrestable, whatever the number.

prompt.text: Does Oregon's DUII law apply to a driver impaired by a prescription medicine?

rationale.text: Oregon's DUII law covers any substance that impairs your mental or physical ability to drive, not just alcohol.

lines.text: Never drive after alcohol or drugs.

narration.text: Never drive after drinking alcohol or using other drugs, because they raise your chance of a collision that can cause serious injury or death. If you have been drinking or using drugs, let someone else drive. That is the starting point for this lesson. From there we look at what DUII means in Oregon, the blood alcohol concentration at which the law presumes you are impaired, why you can still be arrested below that level, how alcohol and marijuana are involved in Oregon collisions, and why medicines are part of the same picture.

lines.text: Affected by alcohol or drugs: DUII.
Presumed impaired at zero point zero eight percent.

narration.text: Driving while alcohol or drugs are affecting you can get you arrested for DUII. Oregon law presumes you are impaired at a blood alcohol concentration of zero point zero eight percent or more. But you can still be arrested with a blood alcohol concentration below zero point zero eight percent. So zero point zero eight percent is the level where impairment is presumed, not a safe limit below which you are protected. The deciding question for an arrest is whether alcohol or drugs are affecting your driving, at whatever level.

lines.text: Below the level is not a safe zone.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A driver believes that staying below zero point zero eight percent means there is nothing to worry about. At zero point zero eight percent or more the law presumes impairment, yet a driver below that level can still be arrested for DUII if alcohol or drugs are affecting their driving. So the number is not a permission slip. The only safe choice the manual gives is not to drive after drinking alcohol or using other drugs at all, and to let someone else drive instead. Keep that rule in mind. That is the rule to remember.

Alcohol is the drug most often involved in impaired driving. Marijuana impairment has also contributed to many Oregon collisions, and using the two together further reduces your ability to drive. Over-the-counter and prescription medicines can also impair driving, so ask a doctor or pharmacist about side effects. If you are unsure whether it is safe to drive after starting a new medicine, use other transportation. And Oregon's DUII law covers any substance that impairs your mental or physical ability to drive, not just alcohol.

Here is a quick check: a driver takes a prescription medicine that impairs their ability to drive. Does Oregon's DUII law apply? The answer is yes. Oregon's DUII law covers any substance that impairs your mental or physical ability to drive, not just alcohol. That is why the manual tells you to ask a doctor or pharmacist about side effects, and to use other transportation if you are unsure after starting a new medicine. Being affected is what matters, whether the substance is alcohol, marijuana, another drug or a medicine.

lines.text: Zero point zero eight is presumed, not safe.

narration.text: To wrap up: never drive after drinking alcohol or using other drugs, and let someone else drive. Driving while affected can get you arrested for DUII. The law presumes impairment at a blood alcohol concentration of zero point zero eight percent or more, but you can be arrested below that level too. Alcohol is the drug most often involved, marijuana has contributed to many Oregon collisions, and the two together reduce your ability further. Medicines can impair as well, and Oregon's DUII law covers any substance that impairs your ability to drive.

why_how.text: By driving in Oregon you have already agreed to testing, and refusing has its own penalties.
The test fail level depends on your age, and the open container law has a strict definition of open.

scenario.text: A twenty-year-old driver has had one drink and is asked to take a breath test.

reasoning.text: Oregon has a zero tolerance law: a driver under twenty-one fails the test with a blood alcohol concentration of any amount.

result.text: The driver fails the test with any amount of alcohol, because they are under twenty-one.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking refusing the test avoids any penalty.

correction.text: Refusing the implied consent test is not a way out, since refusal itself can bring a fine and a suspension of driving privileges.

memory_support.text: Under twenty-one means zero; broken seal means open.

prompt.text: A bottle of wine was opened and then recorked. Under the open container law, is it open or closed?

rationale.text: A container counts as open once its seal is broken, even if it has been closed again, and any open container belongs in the trunk.

narration.text: This lesson covers three Oregon laws. The Implied Consent law says what you have agreed to simply by driving. The zero tolerance law and the adult fail level set the blood alcohol concentrations at which you fail the test, and those levels depend on your age. And the Open Container law says what you may not have in a vehicle on any road, with a strict definition of what counts as open. Each law has a number or a definition you need to know exactly, so we will take them one at a time and then compare. Keep that rule in mind.

lines.text: Driving means you agreed to a test.

narration.text: Under Oregon's Implied Consent law, driving a motor vehicle means you have agreed to take a breath, blood or urine test when a police officer asks. Refusing an implied consent test can bring a fine, a suspension of your driving privileges, or both. So the agreement is made when you drive, not when the officer asks. Refusing the implied consent test is not a way out, since refusal itself can bring a fine and a suspension of driving privileges. Knowing that ahead of time removes any idea that refusal is a safe option. Keep that rule in mind.

lines.text: Twenty-one or over: zero point zero eight percent.

narration.text: Oregon has a zero tolerance law: a driver under twenty-one fails the test with a blood alcohol concentration of any amount. A driver aged twenty-one or over fails the test with a blood alcohol concentration of zero point zero eight percent or more. So the implied consent fail level is any amount of alcohol for a driver under twenty-one, but zero point zero eight percent or more for a driver twenty-one or older. The age line is twenty-one, and the two levels on either side of it are very different, which is why the zero tolerance rule matters so much for young drivers.

lines.text: Illegal in a vehicle on any road.
Open containers go in the trunk.

narration.text: Oregon's Open Container law makes it illegal to have an open bottle or other container of alcohol in a vehicle on any road. A container counts as open once its seal is broken, even if it has been closed again. Any open container belongs in the trunk. So a bottle that was opened and then recapped is still open under the law, and the place for it is the trunk, not the passenger area. The test is whether the seal is broken, not whether the cap is back on, and open containers belong in the trunk. Keep that rule in mind. That is the rule to remember.

Here is the trap. A driver thinks that refusing the breath test means there is no evidence and therefore no penalty. The manual says otherwise. Refusing the implied consent test is not a way out, since refusal itself can bring a fine and a suspension of driving privileges. And by driving a motor vehicle in Oregon, you have already agreed to take a breath, blood or urine test when a police officer asks. So refusing does not undo the agreement you made by driving; it brings its own fine and suspension. Keep that rule in mind.

Here is a quick check: after a picnic, a bottle of wine was opened, partly poured, and then recorked. Under Oregon's Open Container law, is it open or closed? The answer is open. A container counts as open once its seal is broken, even if it has been closed again. So it may not ride in the passenger area of a vehicle on any road. Open alcohol containers should ride in the trunk, and that is where this bottle belongs for the drive home. The seal, not the cork, decides whether a container is open. Keep that rule in mind. That is the rule to remember.

lines.text: Driving means consent; refusal has penalties.

narration.text: To finish: by driving in Oregon you have agreed to a breath, blood or urine test when a police officer asks, and refusing can bring a fine, a suspension, or both. A driver under twenty-one fails the test with any amount of alcohol, and a driver twenty-one or over fails at zero point zero eight percent or more. An open bottle or container of alcohol is illegal in a vehicle on any road, a container is open once its seal is broken even if recapped, and any open container belongs in the trunk. Keep that rule in mind. That is the rule to remember.

why_how.text: Riding outside the cab is discouraged for everyone and illegal for minors, with a separate rule for dogs.
A blowout is a sudden emergency with one response for front and rear tires.

scenario.text: You feel the back of your car start to weave and sway on the highway.

reasoning.text: A rear blowout makes the back of the vehicle weave or sway, and after any blowout you grip the wheel firmly, slow down gradually and pull off the road.

result.text: You grip the wheel firmly, ease off gradually and pull off the road.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a blowout calls for hard braking.

correction.text: After a blowout you grip the steering wheel firmly, slow down gradually and pull off the road.

prompt.text: May a sixteen-year-old ride in the open bed of a pickup in Oregon?

rationale.text: Oregon law forbids anyone under eighteen from riding on a hood, fender, running board, pickup bed or other outside part of a vehicle.

lines.text: Who may ride outside the cab.
What to do when a tire blows.

narration.text: This lesson covers two topics. The first is riding on the outside of a vehicle, including the pickup bed, with different rules for adults, for anyone under eighteen and for dogs. The second is vehicle equipment, starting with maintenance and then the emergency of a tire blowout, including how a front blowout and a rear blowout feel different but call for the same response. Both topics come with short, firm rules in the manual, and both are easy to remember once you see how the pieces fit together. Keep that rule in mind.

lines.text: Dogs need a carrier or framework.

narration.text: No one of any age should ride in a pickup bed or on any outside part of a vehicle. Oregon law forbids anyone under eighteen from riding on a hood, fender, running board, pickup bed or other outside part of a vehicle. A dog may ride on an outside part of a vehicle, including a pickup bed, only if a framework, carrier or other device keeps it from falling off. So riding outside the cab is discouraged for everyone but outlawed for anyone under eighteen, while a dog may ride outside only when a carrier or framework keeps it from falling.

lines.text: Front: hard steering, pull to one side.

narration.text: Good maintenance prevents most equipment failures, an unmaintained vehicle can become unsafe, and your owner's manual lists the maintenance it needs. When a tire does fail, the signs depend on which tire. A front tire blowout makes steering hard and can pull the vehicle strongly to one side, while a rear blowout makes the back of the vehicle weave or sway. After a blowout, grip the steering wheel firmly, slow down gradually and pull off the road. The response is the same for both: grip, slow gradually, pull off. Keep that rule in mind.

lines.text: Do not brake hard after a blowout.

narration.text: Here is the trap. When a tire blows, the instinct is to stomp on the brakes. The manual's response is different: grip the steering wheel firmly, slow down gradually and pull off the road. Whether the blowout is in front, with hard steering and a pull to one side, or in the rear, with the back of the vehicle weaving or swaying, the response is the same. Gradual is the key word. A firm grip and a gradual slowdown, followed by pulling off the road, is the full response to either kind of blowout. Keep that rule in mind. That is the rule to remember.

Here is a quick check: a sixteen-year-old wants to ride in the open bed of a friend's pickup truck. Is that allowed in Oregon? The answer is no. Oregon law forbids anyone under eighteen from riding on a hood, fender, running board, pickup bed or other outside part of a vehicle. And the manual adds that no one of any age should ride there. The only outside rider the manual allows with conditions is a dog, and only if a framework, carrier or other device keeps it from falling off the vehicle. Keep that rule in mind. That is the rule to remember.

To wrap up: no one of any age should ride in a pickup bed or on the outside of a vehicle, Oregon law forbids it for anyone under eighteen, and a dog may ride outside only if a framework, carrier or other device keeps it from falling. Good maintenance prevents most equipment failures. A front blowout makes steering hard and pulls to one side, a rear blowout makes the back weave or sway, and for either one you grip the wheel firmly, slow down gradually and pull off the road. Keep that rule in mind. That is the rule to remember.

why_how.text: Brake, headlight, power steering and accelerator failures each have a specific response sequence.
Two of the sequences are easy to confuse, and fuel-saving habits round out the lesson.

scenario.text: The accelerator sticks while you are driving on a city street.

reasoning.text: If the accelerator sticks, look for an escape path and shift into neutral, using an open palm on the shifter so you do not push it into another gear.

result.text: You shift to neutral with an open palm, steer smoothly while braking, and leave the road once it is safe.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking failed brakes and a stuck accelerator call for the same steps.

correction.text: Failed brakes call for pumping the pedal and downshifting, whereas a stuck accelerator calls for shifting to neutral and braking while steering smoothly.

memory_support.text: Brakes gone: pump, downshift. Pedal stuck: neutral.

prompt.text: Your brakes fail. What is the first thing to try?

rationale.text: If your brakes fail, pump the pedal, which may build enough pressure to get them working again.

lines.text: Each failure has its own steps.
Know them before you need them.

narration.text: Even well maintained vehicles can have equipment fail while you are driving. This lesson goes through the manual's response for each failure it names: brakes that stop working, headlights that go out, power steering that fails and an accelerator that sticks. Each one has a short sequence of steps. Two of them, failed brakes and a stuck accelerator, are easy to mix up because both are about speed you cannot control, so we will compare them directly. At the end, the lesson closes with the manual's simple fuel-saving habits.

If your brakes fail, pump the pedal, which may build enough pressure to get them working again. Shift to a lower gear so the engine helps slow the vehicle, and apply the parking brake slowly. Warn other drivers with your horn or lights that you cannot control the vehicle, and once you have slowed, ease onto the shoulder. So the sequence is pump, downshift, parking brake applied slowly, warn others, and ease onto the shoulder once you have slowed. Each step adds a little more slowing or a little more warning to the drivers around you.

lines.text: Headlights: flip the switch, try other lights.
Both: slow and ease onto the shoulder.

narration.text: If your headlights go out, flip the headlight switch off and on, then try your high beams, driving lights or hazard lights, which may give enough light to steer off the road. After a headlight failure, slow down and ease onto the shoulder. If power steering fails, grip the wheel firmly because steering will be hard, then slow down and ease onto the shoulder. So both of these failures end the same way, slowing and easing onto the shoulder, with headlights adding the switch and other lights, and power steering adding a firm grip.

If the accelerator sticks, look for an escape path and shift into neutral, using an open palm on the shifter so you do not push it into another gear. With a stuck accelerator, steer smoothly while braking and leave the road once it is safe. The open palm detail is there for a reason the manual states: it keeps you from pushing the shifter past neutral into another gear. So the sequence is escape path, neutral with an open palm, smooth steering while braking, and leaving the road once it is safe to do so. Keep that rule in mind.

Here is the trap. Both of these failures feel like losing control of your speed, so drivers mix up the steps. Failed brakes call for pumping the pedal and downshifting, whereas a stuck accelerator calls for shifting to neutral and braking while steering smoothly. So with failed brakes the steps are pump the pedal, shift to a lower gear, apply the parking brake slowly, warn others and ease onto the shoulder. With a stuck accelerator the steps are find an escape path, shift to neutral with an open palm, steer smoothly while braking and leave the road once it is safe.

Here is a quick check: you press the brake pedal and nothing happens. What is the first thing to try? The answer is to pump the brake pedal, which may build enough pressure to get the brakes working again. After that, shift to a lower gear so the engine helps slow the vehicle, apply the parking brake slowly, warn other drivers with your horn or lights, and once you have slowed, ease onto the shoulder. Do not confuse this with a stuck accelerator, where the first move is to shift into neutral with an open palm. Keep that rule in mind.

lines.text: No jackrabbit starts or sudden stops.
Less idling, fewer trips, good upkeep.

narration.text: The manual also lists simple ways to save fuel. Drive at a steady pace without going over posted limits, and avoid jackrabbit starts and sudden stops. Other fuel savers are cutting unneeded idling, combining errands into one trip and keeping the vehicle properly maintained. Notice that maintenance appears twice in this section of the manual: it prevents most equipment failures, and it also helps save fuel. A steady, smooth driving style and a well kept vehicle serve both goals at once, along with planning your trips to cut down on idling and extra driving.

To wrap up the equipment failures: for failed brakes, pump the pedal, shift to a lower gear, apply the parking brake slowly, warn others with horn or lights, and ease onto the shoulder once slowed. For a stuck accelerator, find an escape path, shift to neutral with an open palm, steer smoothly while braking, and leave the road once safe. For headlights, flip the switch and try other lights; for power steering, grip firmly; then slow down and ease onto the shoulder. And to save fuel, drive steadily within the limits, idle less and combine errands.
